interview_questions.q: How do you architect a multi-tenant SaaS database?
interview_questions.a: Three patterns: (1) Row-level security (one shared schema, tenant_id column with PostgreSQL RLS policies — simplest operationally, suitable for most SaaS). (2) Schema-per-tenant (separate PostgreSQL schema per tenant — good isolation, moderately complex migrations). (3) Database-per-tenant (maximum isolation, highest cost, only for enterprise clients with data residency requirements). My default: row-level security with PostgreSQL RLS. It scales to thousands of tenants, simplifies migrations, and provides strong isolation with proper policy enforcement.

interview_questions.q: How do you debug a slow API endpoint in production?
interview_questions.a: Systematic process: (1) Check Sentry/Prometheus for p95/p99 latency — is it consistently slow or occasional spikes? (2) EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the slowest queries (pg_stat_statements shows top queries by total_time). (3) Check for N+1 queries in SQLAlchemy ORM — add relationship loading strategies. (4) Check Redis cache hit rate — is the caching layer being bypassed? (5) Profile the FastAPI endpoint with py-spy if CPU-bound. (6) Check external API calls — are third-party integrations adding latency? Systematic elimination, not guessing.

interview_questions.q: What is your approach to handling authentication in a Next.js + FastAPI application?
interview_questions.a: Next.js handles auth sessions (Auth.js/NextAuth with PostgreSQL adapter). FastAPI validates JWT tokens on every protected endpoint (python-jose). Access tokens: short-lived (15min), stored in memory. Refresh tokens: long-lived (7 days), HTTP-only secure cookie (not localStorage). API routes in Next.js act as BFF (Backend for Frontend) — proxying requests with credentials, not exposing JWT to the browser directly. Rate limiting on auth endpoints (5 attempts/minute). Refresh token rotation on every use.

interview_questions.q: How do you implement real-time features in a full stack application?
interview_questions.a: Options: (1) Server-Sent Events (SSE) — best for one-directional real-time (AI response streaming, notifications, live feeds). Simple, HTTP/1.1 compatible, auto-reconnects. FastAPI natively supports SSE with async generators. (2) WebSockets — bidirectional real-time (chat, collaborative editing, gaming). Higher complexity, requires connection state management. (3) Polling — simplest, highest latency, highest server load. Only for low-frequency updates. My default: SSE for AI streaming and notifications, WebSockets for collaborative features. Both handled in FastAPI with connection manager and Redis pub/sub for multi-instance scaling.
